resolved_by: Supreme Court, Esteras v. United States (2025), which held that a district court may not consider the § 3553(a)(2)(A) retribution factor when revoking supervised release under § 3583(e). Decided after this opinion; the excerpt itself does not mention it.
issue: When revoking supervised release under 18 U.S.C. § 3583(e), may a district court consider the § 3553(a)(2)(A) retributive factors, which § 3583(e) does not list?

sides.position: Considering § 3553(a)(2)(A) factors when revoking supervised release is not reversible error, even though § 3583(e) does not enumerate them.
cases: United States v. Lewis, 498 F.3d 393 (6th Cir. 2007)
United States v. Esteras, 88 F.4th 1170 (6th Cir. 2023)

sides.position: Consideration of § 3553(a)(2)(A) factors is procedural error when they are a dominant or undue factor in the revocation sentence, or revocation based principally on them is procedurally unreasonable.
cases: United States v. Young, 634 F.3d 233 (3d Cir. 2011)
United States v. Rivera, 784 F.3d 1012 (5th Cir. 2015)
United States v. Miqbel, 444 F.3d 1173 (9th Cir. 2006)
United States v. Booker, 63 F.4th 1254 (10th Cir. 2023)

this_court: does not decide (the excerpted dissent criticizes the Sixth Circuit's position, which permits such consideration)
quote: Though there is a circuit split on this issue, most circuits would find that a revocation of supervised release principally based on the § 3553(a)(2)(A) factors is procedurally unreasonable.
cite: United States v. Edgardo Esteras, 88 F.4th 1170 (6th Cir. 2023)
